title: Check a link's kind and direction
statement: When content links two facts, check that the stated kind and direction of the link hold, not only that the facts are related.
example: About 20 of the 160 generated links people rejected were wrong in kind, direction or claim, such as one that ran the other way around.
detail: People checked 2,087 model-generated links between knowledge nodes for an AP history course and marked 160 'No'. About 20 of the rejection notes concern the link's kind, direction or claim: one idea inspired rather than enabled another, 'included' was the right term instead of 'enabled', a link ran 'more the other way around', or one fact did not exemplify the other. Rejection rates by stated type ran from 4.2% for 'causes' (6 of 143) to 9.1% for 'exemplifies' (76 of 835).
against: Most generated links were kept, and repeats, not wrong kinds of link, were the commoner reason for rejection, so the per-type rates are driven mostly by repeats.

correct a false causal implication in the current student question.
Current source says “The Lost Boys scrambled for their weapons, but they were outnumbered.”
The keyed answer describes the numerical disadvantage they faced, not something caused by reaching for weapons.
Both rubric and uses-but-so criterion say “Uses at least one But and one So to join an event to its consequence.” So can signal a result; but signals contrast.
L7 second_hint “the boys were armed, so they charged. Peter fought Hook, but Hook fell” is a poor contrast because Hook falling is the expected fight result.
Both lessons' connective requirements distinguish contrast from result.
Asks what happened as a result of scrambling for weapons; key says pirates outnumbered them, while source uses contrast but.
L6/L7 But/So rubric treats contrast as consequence; L7 hint uses expected fight outcome as contrast.
The boys reaching for weapons does not cause pirates to outnumber them; being outnumbered is the obstacle already present.
